claims.title: Fleet-key telemetry flooding can saturate the shared Pub/Sub ingestion path
claims.description: A party that obtains the fleet-wide pre-shared key from any deployed node can send a high volume of otherwise accepted readings through `flow:entity:sensor-node>process:device-gateway>publish-readings`. Because the same key is shared by every device and has not been rotated, one usable fleet credential can make `process:device-gateway` forward attacker volume over `flow:process:device-gateway>store:pub-sub>forward-readings` into `store:pub-sub`. If Pub/Sub ingress quotas, retention budgets, subscriber backpressure, and per-device message limits are not configured, the attacker spends messages while exhausting shared broker throughput or quota. Second-order, `process:telemetry-normalizer` cannot keep up with or consume legitimate readings over `flow:process:telemetry-normalizer>store:pub-sub>pick-up-readings`; fresh telemetry is delayed before it can be loaded into `store:telemetry-lake`, affecting fleet-wide analytics and dashboards. This is conditional on the unstated capacity and per-device metering controls.

grounds.text: The key is per fleet, not per device. Nobody has rotated it since deployment.
Readings the gateway accepts are forwarded onto Pub/Sub and picked up by the telemetry normalizer

severity.justification: Likelihood is high because an attacker who extracts the shared, never-rotated fleet key from any physically accessible `entity:sensor-node` can submit accepted traffic through the internet-facing publish flow; impact is high because saturating shared `store:pub-sub` stalls legitimate fleet telemetry before normalizer processing and fleet-wide analytics.

mitigations.summary: Use per-device credentials and per-device ingest quotas
mitigations.detail: Replace the fleet-wide pre-shared key on `flow:entity:sensor-node>process:device-gateway>publish-readings` with rotated per-device credentials, and rate-limit accepted messages by verified device and customer identity.

mitigations.summary: Bound Pub/Sub backlog and isolate abusive producers
mitigations.detail: Set explicit ingress, retention, and cost budgets for `store:pub-sub`; use per-tenant topics or quotas, bounded subscriptions, and gateway load shedding so one device or fleet cannot consume the normalizer's shared capacity.

mitigations.summary: Make consumer overload fail predictably
mitigations.detail: Apply bounded concurrency, backpressure, timeouts, and alerting to `process:telemetry-normalizer` so a growing Pub/Sub backlog is detected and shed rather than becoming an unbounded pipeline outage.

recommendation.note: Per-device credentials, verified-device quotas, Pub/Sub backlog limits, producer isolation, and bounded consumer backpressure address the accepted-message flooding path.

claims.title: Shared fleet key enables forged telemetry from a compromised node
claims.description: An attacker who extracts the fleet-wide pre-shared key from a sensor node under their physical control can publish fabricated readings on `flow:entity:sensor-node>process:device-gateway>publish-readings` to `process:device-gateway` as a fleet device. Because the key is shared by every node and has not been rotated, the gateway cannot distinguish a forged device reading from one sent by the claimed device. Second-order, accepted forged readings are written through `store:pub-sub`, consumed by `process:telemetry-normalizer`, and loaded into `store:telemetry-lake`, corrupting customer telemetry, including occupancy patterns used by fleet dashboards.

grounds.text: The key is per fleet, not per device. Nobody has rotated it since deployment.
They are outside our physical control — a technician can be standing next to one with a laptop.
Readings the gateway accepts are forwarded onto Pub/Sub and picked up by the telemetry normalizer, a Python consumer in our analytics network, which writes them into the telemetry lake in BigQuery.

mitigations.summary: Use unique, rotatable device credentials
mitigations.detail: Replace the fleet-wide pre-shared key on `flow:entity:sensor-node>process:device-gateway>publish-readings` with per-device credentials, revocation, and rotation so compromise of one node cannot authorize writes for the fleet.

mitigations.summary: Bind readings to the enrolled device identity
mitigations.detail: Have `process:device-gateway` verify a per-device signature or authenticated device identity and reject readings whose claimed device identifier does not match that identity.

recommendation.note: Per-device credentials and gateway verification of the enrolled device identity directly prevent forged readings under another node identity.

Repeated downloads of firmware images can consume the bucket's request capacity, network egress allocation, or metered budget more cheaply than the service delivers the image data, if no CDN, per-client rate limit, download budget, or egress quota is configured. Second-order, legitimate `entity:sensor-node` instances cannot retrieve updates from `store:firmware-bucket`, delaying fleet-wide firmware deployment and recovery while the resource remains saturated.

claims.title: A sensor node can deny publishing a reading because the fleet credential identifies no individual device
claims.description: Any holder of the fleet-wide pre-shared key can submit readings on `flow:entity:sensor-node>process:device-gateway>publish-readings` to `process:device-gateway`; the credential identifies the fleet rather than a particular `entity:sensor-node`. Consequently, when a reading later affects customer-site records through `flow:process:device-gateway>store:pub-sub>forward-readings`, a node owner or an actor with access to the shared key can plausibly deny having originated it because the gateway's authentication evidence cannot distinguish them from any other device. This is an accountability gap, not a claim that the actor forged or altered a reading. Second-order, disputed readings can undermine the evidential value of telemetry later loaded by `process:telemetry-normalizer` into `store:telemetry-lake`, which holds `pii` and `business-critical-data`.

grounds.text: The key is per fleet, not per device.

Impact is medium because the disputed readings reach `store:telemetry-lake`, which is tagged `pii` and `business-critical-data`, affecting the reliability of customer telemetry records without disclosing or destroying them by this threat alone.

Impact is low because the model states that the session carries device configuration and diagnostics, but assigns no sensitive asset tag or broader administrative authority to `entity:sensor-node`.

mitigations.summary: Require unique technician authentication for serial servicing
mitigations.detail: Make `flow:entity:field-technician>entity:sensor-node>local-service-session` explicitly authenticate a named technician, preferably with phishing-resistant credentials or device-bound service tokens, before granting read-write console access.

mitigations.summary: Limit and audit local service sessions
mitigations.detail: Require time-limited authorization for each node, restrict service commands to the maintenance role, and record the authenticated technician and actions locally or on reconnection.

recommendation.note: Explicit named-technician authentication, scoped service authorization, and session auditing address the conditional impersonation path.

claims.title: An attacker could consume telemetry as the normalizer if Pub/Sub caller authentication is absent
claims.description: `flow:process:telemetry-normalizer>store:pub-sub>pick-up-readings` crosses from `boundary:analytics-core` to `boundary:ingest-edge` with `authentication: unknown`. If that unknown resolves to no verified workload identity and authorization, an attacker with a foothold able to reach the ingest-side endpoint could impersonate `process:telemetry-normalizer` to `store:pub-sub` and consume readings as the normalizer. This is conditional on the unverified authentication attribute. Second-order: the consumed messages contain normalized sensor readings tagged `pii`, and the genuine normalizer loads those readings into `store:telemetry-lake`.

verdict.reason: The claim depends on whether the normalizer-to-Pub/Sub flow authenticates and authorizes the consuming workload.

severity.justification: Likelihood is low and conditional because `unknown:flow:process:telemetry-normalizer>store:pub-sub>pick-up-readings:authentication` leaves the control unverified, but exploitation also requires a foothold that can reach the ingest-side endpoint across the derived crossing. Impact is medium because `store:pub-sub` and the flow carry `pii` readings, and the normalizer's downstream destination `store:telemetry-lake` is confidential and tagged `pii`.

mitigations.summary: Use an explicit workload identity for Pub/Sub consumption
mitigations.detail: Configure `flow:process:telemetry-normalizer>store:pub-sub>pick-up-readings` with an authenticated, unique normalizer workload identity and grant it only the required subscription-consume permission.

mitigations.summary: Record and verify subscription authorization
mitigations.detail: Establish whether authentication is currently enforced for this flow; if it is not, require a verifiable service credential and restrict Pub/Sub access to the normalizer's designated subscription.

recommendation.note: A unique workload identity with restricted subscription-consume permission addresses impersonation of the normalizer.

rejected_claims.title: MQTT connection and authentication floods can exhaust the internet-facing gateway
rejected_claims.description: An internet attacker can flood `process:device-gateway` over `flow:entity:sensor-node>process:device-gateway>publish-readings` with MQTT connection and authentication attempts. The gateway is exposed to the internet and checks presented node keys through `flow:process:device-gateway>store:device-registry>look-up-device`; consequently, attacker-controlled connection volume can consume gateway connection/worker capacity and drive repeated registry lookups before legitimate nodes can publish. The model does not state per-source connection limits, authentication-attempt budgets, idle timeouts, or load shedding, so this risk is conditional on those controls not bounding the work. Second-order, legitimate readings cannot enter the pipeline, preventing `process:device-gateway` from forwarding accepted telemetry to `store:pub-sub` and delaying downstream normalization and lake loading.

grounds.text: an MQTT broker we run on GKE and expose to the internet because the nodes dial in from anywhere.
The gateway looks up the device in a device registry (Firestore) to check the key

verdict.reason: Duplicate of D-02: both describe flooding the gateway through `flow:entity:sensor-node>process:device-gateway>publish-readings`, but D-02 more completely covers the accepted-message path, shared Pub/Sub saturation, and downstream fleet-wide availability impact.

severity.justification: Likelihood is high because `process:device-gateway` is internet-exposed and `flow:entity:sensor-node>process:device-gateway>publish-readings` crosses from `boundary:field-network` into the ingest edge, allowing arbitrary remote attackers to attempt MQTT sessions. Impact is medium because the immediate result is a recoverable fleet-ingest outage, but it blocks legitimate readings from progressing into the shared telemetry pipeline.

mitigations.summary: Bound unauthenticated MQTT work at the gateway
mitigations.detail: Apply per-source connection and authentication-attempt limits, short handshake and idle timeouts, and bounded worker/connection pools with fail-fast load shedding on `process:device-gateway`.

mitigations.summary: Protect registry lookup capacity
mitigations.detail: Cache bounded successful device-resolution results where appropriate and enforce gateway-side admission control so unauthenticated MQTT attempts cannot generate unbounded calls on `flow:process:device-gateway>store:device-registry>look-up-device`.
